title: Living in Norway | The Truth About Life in the World's Richest and Most Beautiful Country | 4K
fullText: [music] >> On a snowy street in Norway at 8:00 on a January morning, a 7-year-old walks to school alone in the dark and not one adult who passes finds this worrying. >> [music] >> She lives in the richest country on Earth. Though you would never by looking. No supercars, no mansions on display. [music] Her nation quietly owns a share of nearly every company [music] on the planet. Yet it keeps an unwritten law against showing off and breaking that law is the closest thing this country has to a sin. [music] To understand how a place gets this rich and stays this quiet, a visit is not enough. You have to stay a full year. So that is what we [music] will do. From the January fish to the December lights. The year begins in the far north above the Arctic Circle where the Lofoten Islands rise out of the sea like a wall of broken teeth. It is the coldest, darkest opening of any calendar [music] in Europe and it is exactly when this coast comes alive. Every January, millions of Arctic cod leave the Barents Sea and swim south to spawn in these waters. The migration is so old and so reliable that the fish carries its own name, skrei, from an ancient Norse word meaning [music] to move forward. The season runs from January to April, and coastal families have planned entire lives around it. For a thousand years, boats have gone out to meet them. >> [music] >> In villages like Henningsvær and Svolvær, the catch is split, salted, or hung in pairs on huge wooden racks >> [music] >> and left to the wind. That is the entire recipe. No salt required, no fuel, just freezing air and time until the fish becomes stockfish, hard as wood and good for years. The racks stand along the shore like timber cathedrals, and in February [music] and March, whole villages smell of the sea drying into money. >> [music] >> Centuries before anyone here had heard the word oil, this dried cod was Norway's gold. It fed Europe through Lent, paid for churches and ships, and taught a poor country at the edge of the map how to trade with the world. In Henningsvær, a fishing village scattered across a cluster of islets, the drying racks share the shoreline with a football pitch wedged between the rocks, one of the most photographed sports fields on Earth. Fish below, football in the middle, mountains over everything. Nobody planned the composition. It is simply what a working coast looks like after a thousand years. The fisherman's cabins along the shore are all the same deep red, and there are two explanations. The practical one is that red paint mixed from cheap ochre and cod liver oil was simply the cheapest color a fisherman could buy. The older one is that a red wall is the last thing you can still see from a boat when the snow comes down sideways. Both are true, and both say the same thing about this country. Nothing here was ever built to be admired. It was built to survive, and it became beautiful by accident. >> [music] >> The sea made Norway tough, but what really made it rich lies under a different part of that sea, and we will get there in June. First, the darkness deserves a chapter of its own. >> [music] [music] >> In Tromsø, the largest city of the Norwegian Arctic, the sun goes down in late November and does not rise again until the middle of January. Even in February, it barely clears [music] the mountains. >> [music] >> Noon is a long blue twilight, and here is the honest part, the part the postcards skip. >> [music] >> The dark is genuinely hard. Winter weighs on mood and energy. Doctors here take the season seriously, and in many homes, a light [music] therapy lamp sits on the kitchen counter as casually as a toaster. >> [bell] [music] >> Some mornings the alarm rings into blackness, the school run happens under stars, and the will to get up has to be manufactured by hand. Norwegians will not pretend otherwise, because pretending is not their style. >> [music] >> What they have done instead may be the most Norwegian thing of all. They built a culture designed [music] to make the darkness worth having. The word for it is koselig, [music] usually translated as cozy, but that translation is too small. Koselig is a strategy. [music] It is candles lit at breakfast, wool socks by the door, bread in the oven, friends around a table [music] with no plan to leave. It is the deliberate manufacture of warmth in the exact months that warmth is scarce. Cafes compete on [music] candlelight. Offices keep blankets. An invitation [music] that elsewhere would say come for dinner says here, come be warm with us. >> [music] >> Researchers who came to this city expecting an epidemic of winter depression [music] found something quieter instead. Many locals do not endure the polar night. They look forward [music] to it, the way other people look forward to summer. They even have a name for the season's payoff, >> [music] >> mørketid, the dark time, when the sky above the rooftops opens into curtains of green and violet light. >> [music] >> The aurora is not a tourist attraction here. It is a household event. Someone shouts from the balcony, dinner gets cold, and an entire [music] street stands in the snow looking up. >> [music] >> A country that can teach itself to love a two-month night can handle almost anything, >> [music] >> including, as it turns out, an ordinary Tuesday, which is where Norway quietly becomes most [music] impressive of all. March in Trondheim, the medieval capital in the middle of the country, and the light is coming back fast. Follow one family through one unremarkable day because the unremarkable days are where this [music] country hides its miracles. The children leave first, on foot [music] and by bicycle, and mostly without adults. A 7-year-old crossing town alone is not neglect here. It is the standard. Along parts of the coast, >> [music] >> some children even ride a boat to school the way others ride a bus. Ask a Norwegian [music] parent how they dare, and they will look puzzled because the question assumes a world >> [music] >> they do not live in. The entire society functions as one enormous pair of watching, benevolent eyes. >> [music] >> People who moved here from bigger, warier countries describe the moment it clicks, usually the first time their own child asks to walk somewhere alone, and they [music] hear themselves, to their amazement, saying yes. >> [bell] >> The adults are at work by 8:00 and this is the part that breaks foreign visitors [music] most of them are walking out again between half past 3:00 and 5:00. Overtime is not a badge of honor here. It is treated as a planning failure. The working week is 37 and 1/2 hours. Five weeks of vacation are written into law. And yet Norwegian productivity per hour stands among the highest on Earth. The quiet logic underneath, a rested person works better. Parents who see their children raise [music] better ones. And no email was ever worth a childhood. At lunch, offices empty for a walk outside in any weather because of a word that needs no translation by now, friluftsliv, the open-air life, less a hobby than a mild national religion. [music] And when a baby arrives, the state hands the parents roughly a year of paid leave to divide between them. Father included, expected, and unembarrassed. [music] Push a stroller through Trondheim on a weekday morning and half the people strollers beside you are men. Raising a family [music] here, people say, feels less like a private struggle and more like being carried by something large and calm. The word they reach for is trust. It will come back at the end of this [music] year because it turns out to be the answer to the entire riddle. >> In April, Norway performs its great annual vanishing act. It is Easter week and the city's simply empty. Shops close, streets fall silent and the entire nation migrates upward above the tree line >> [music] >> into the snow. They are going to the height, the mountain cabin, and no single object explains Norway better. Roughly a third of families own one and close to half have keys to one somewhere through parents, cousins, or friends. [music] The classic hytte is small, wooden, and deliberately inconvenient. [music] Wi-Fi is weak or absent on purpose. Water [music] may come from a well. Warmth comes from wood. You split yourself >> [music] >> and that is precisely the point. In most countries, the rich display wealth with marble and glass. In Norway, [music] a millionaire's proudest possession is a plain pine cabin where everyone washes dishes by hand. The value, Norwegians will tell you, was never in luxury. It is in the fire, the silence, and the absence [music] of anywhere else to be. Many cabins have passed through the same family for three or four generations and the neighboring cabins have too. Children grow up seeing the same [music] faces every Easter of their lives at the same altitude doing the same blessed nothing. >> [music] >> Easter itself runs on rituals so specific they sound invented. Cross-country skis, learned in childhood almost alongside walking. Oranges, eaten in the snow by the bagful. And a red, >> [music] >> yellow, and green chocolate bar called Kvikklunsj, of which Norwegians eat some 20 million in this one week, a third of the entire year's supply, almost all of it on mountainsides. >> [music] >> Strangest of all, Easter is crime season. Publishers time their murder mysteries [music] for it. Newspapers print holiday whodunits. And the tradition has its own name, Påskekrim, Easter [music and clears throat] crime. A nation of gentle, law-abiding people >> [music] >> sitting peacefully in cabins reading about murder. Nobody can fully explain it. Nobody wants to change it, either. By the end of the week, they ski home. Sunburned in the strange way of snow and spring light. May is coming. >> [music] >> And May is when this quiet country allows itself, once a year, to be loud. On the 17th [music] of May, Norway holds its national day. And it does something almost no other country does. There are no tanks. There are no missiles rolling past a podium. Instead, in every town, from Bergen to the smallest fjord village, the parade is made of children, marching bands of them, waving flags, singing at the top [music] of their lungs, while the adults line the streets and cheer. In Bergen, it will very possibly be raining because in Bergen, it is usually raining. And the parade will simply happen wet. Umbrellas up, trumpets slightly out of tune, absolutely nobody going home. A national day built around school children instead of soldiers tells you nearly everything about what this country decided to become. The other thing you notice is the clothing. On this one day, Norwegians step out in the bunad, the traditional costume [music] of their home region. And a bunad is not a costume in any casual sense. Each one is hand-sewn, loaded with silver, and encoded like a map. Embroidered roses in red and green mean Hardanger. Black wool with gleaming silver buckles means Setesdal. A trained eye can read a crowd and tell you which valley every family came from three generations back. A full bunad costs anywhere from two to $5,000, sometimes more. And it may be the only visibly expensive thing a Norwegian ever wears in public. The unwritten law against showing off makes one single exception per year, and this is it because a bunad does not say, "Look at me." It says, "Look where I am from." The day they are celebrating is the constitution of 1814. But the joy has a sharper edge to it than that. Norway spent 400 years under Danish rule, then most of a century under Sweden, and only in 1905 did it walk away as a fully independent state. Young, poor, and unnoticed by the world. Barely two generations later, the unnoticed little country won a kind of lottery no one saw coming. That story begins in the June chapter off the coast of a modest town that used to can sardines. Stavanger, on the southwest coast, was for most [music] of its history a town that fished and canned sardines. Then, in the autumn of 1969, an American drilling crew working for Phillips Petroleum hit something [music] enormous under the North Sea. On the 23rd of December, the company formally told the Norwegian government what it now owned. One of the largest oil fields ever discovered >> [music] >> anywhere. The country got the news two days before Christmas. It has been calling the discovery a Christmas present ever since. And remember that phrase, because this story will end at Christmas, too. >> [music] >> What Norway did next is the part historians still marvel at. It did not hand the seabed to foreign companies, and it did not spend the money. It taxed the oil hard, built its own expertise, and beginning in the '90s, poured [music] the profits into a national savings account with one sacred rule. The fund is for everyone, including Norwegians who have not been born yet, and the government may spend no more than around 3% of it in any year. Half a century of that discipline has produced the largest sovereign wealth fund on Earth, now worth over $2 trillion. >> [music] >> It holds stakes in more than 7,000 companies, roughly 1 and 1/2% of every listed share on the planet. Buy an index fund anywhere in the world, and you are in a small way doing business with Norway. On paper, it works out to around $400,000 for every citizen, from the king to the newest baby in Tromsø. Nobody can touch it. That is the point. Here is the honest arithmetic of daily life, because wealth like that still comes with a bill. Gasoline in Norway costs more than almost anywhere on Earth, by design, in the country that exports the stuff. A beer at an Oslo bar costs what a meal costs elsewhere. Rents in the capital rank among Europe's steepest, and income taxes bite hard. What comes back is specific, and Norwegians can list it from memory. University, free. Healthcare, capped at roughly $300 a year out of pocket, and after that, the card in your wallet says free until January. A year of paid parental leave, split between two parents who both actually take it. And the world's fastest escape from the very product that made them rich. In 2025, 96% of all new cars sold in Norway were fully electric. They are using the oil money to build a country that will not need oil. Whether the world sees irony or wisdom in that, Norway has stopped asking. In July, the whole rich machine does something almost unthinkable. It switches itself off. July is Fellesferie, the common holiday, when so much of Norway takes its legally protected vacation at once that the country seems to change owners. Offices go quiet. Out of office replies grow honest, back in August, no exceptions, and 5 weeks of legally protected freedom pour into the fjords, onto the islands, up the mountains in a nationwide exhale that no amount of money has ever convinced Norwegians to skip. To understand what they are looking at, understand what a fjord actually is. The sea did not carve these canyons. Ice did. Glaciers grinding valleys a mile deep [music] over millions of years, and when the ice finally left, the ocean moved in to fill the wound. The Sognefjord, the longest [music] in the country, runs more than 200 km inland, deeper in places than the mountains beside it are tall. Threaded into this landscape are two of Norway's proudest machines and one of its oldest prayers. The Flåm Railway drops from the high plateau to the fjord shore down one of the steepest standard rail lines in the world. The ride is so absurdly scenic that national television once aired an entire train [music] journey across Norway unedited hour after hour. More than a million [music] people tuned in to watch a train simply go. Norwegians named the genre slow TV and they meant it as a compliment. >> [music] >> And in a quiet valley stands the Borgund stave church raised around the year 1180. Built entirely of pine and joined without a single metal nail. [music] Carved dragon heads still snarl from its roof line beside the Christian crosses hedging [music] the young faith against the old gods. Nearly 2,000 of these wooden churches once stood across Norway. 28 remain and Borgund is the one time forgot to touch. There is one more rule that makes a Norwegian summer possible and it may be the most radical law in this book of unwritten ones except this one is written. Allemannsretten, the right to roam. Every mountain, forest, and [music] shore in the country is open to everyone to walk, camp, and pick berries regardless of who [music] owns it. Wealth may own the land here. It is not allowed to fence off the view. >> By September, the light is leaving again and Norway enters its season of keeping. >> [music] >> In Røros, a former copper mining town on a high plateau near the Swedish border, the old instincts are close [music] to the surface. This is one of the coldest inhabited places in the country, a town of tar black timber houses where winter temperatures [music] have gone below minus 50 and for three centuries, its people survived on a simple rule. Whatever autumn gives you, put it away. Meat was salted and smoked. Fish was dried. Root vegetables went into cellars dug deep below the frost line and a family's wealth was measured in what it had put away by October. The town is a UNESCO World Heritage Site now, but the cellars still get filled. Half from thrift, half from something [music] closer to instinct. Norway's strangest delicacy was born from exactly this refusal to waste. In 1863, a young dairy maid named Anne Hov working a summer mountain farm in the Gudbrandsdalen Valley, looked at the whey leftover from cheese making, the part everyone threw away, and decided to pour cream in and keep boiling. It cooked down into a dense caramel [music] brown block that looked like fudge and tasted like nothing else [music] in Europe. Brunost, brown cheese, was born. >> It sold so well that it is credited with pulling her whole valley out of hard times. And today, Norwegians slice it onto their morning bread, the way the rest of the world spreads butter. One farm woman, one pot she refused to empty, one national icon. September is also harvest season for everyone, not just farmers, because the right to roam turns the entire country into a commons. Families disappear into the forests with buckets after blueberries lingonberries mushrooms and the golden prize of the high bogs, the cloudberry, so treasured that Norwegians famously guard their secret picking spots more carefully than their bank codes. The freezers fill. The nights lengthen. And in the far north, the oldest harvest of all is on the move. Up on the Finnmark Plateau, where Norway opens into a treeless ocean of tundra, November means the reindeer are walking. The Sami, the indigenous people of the European Arctic, have herded them across these ranges [music] since long before Norway existed as a state. They move with the seasons, and they carry a culture with its own languages and its own crafts called duodji. They carry music, too. The joik is one of the oldest continuous song traditions in Europe, and it does not work like other songs. A joik is not sung about a person. It is a way of singing the person themselves into the room. For a long [music] century, the Norwegian state tried to erase all of it, banning the language in schools and renaming the children. That policy is now a matter of public apology, taught [music] honestly in the same classrooms that once enforced it. Today, Sami is taught again. A Sami parliament sits in Karasjok, and the joik has been sung on national television by artists who wear the gakti, the traditional dress, like a banner. But the newest chapter is complicated [music] and it belongs in any honest portrait of this country. On the Fosen peninsula, Norway built part of Europe's largest onshore wind farm, clean power for the green transition on winter pastures the reindeer had used for [music] centuries. Reindeer will not graze under the flicker and hum of [music] the blades, and roads now cut the old migration routes. The herders sued. >> [music] >> In 2021, Norway's Supreme Court ruled that the turbines violated the herders' human rights under international law. And then for years, the turbines kept turning anyway, while young Sami activists in traditional [music] dress sat down in the lobbies of government ministries, and protests filled the streets of Oslo. >> [music] >> The government eventually apologized, and compensation agreements followed. [music] New grazing lands, a veto over the wind farm's future. But the blades still spin above Fosen today. And the question they carved into this country has not gone away. Even clean energy has to stand >> [music] >> on someone's land. A nation that owns $2 trillion is still learning what it cannot buy back. December, and the year [music] closes where the money lives, in Oslo. The capital of the richest country per person in [music] the developed world looks in the dark of a December afternoon almost defiantly ordinary. Advent stars glow in apartment windows. Christmas markets sell gløgg and gingerbread. [music] The julbord season fills restaurants with office parties. What you will not find is the theater of wealth. No forest of supercars, no gated [music] palaces, no logos worn like armor. The executive [music] and the electrician stand in the same ski trail queue in the same [music] weather proof jacket. And telling them apart is genuinely difficult. Their children attend [music] the same schools. Their mothers wait in the same clinics. The man who manages the $2 trillion fund rides to work through the same weather as everyone else. There is a name for the force behind this, and it did not come from a king or a church. It came from a novel. In 1933, [music] the writer Aksel Sandemose, invented a small [music] fictional town called Jante and gave it 10 mocking commandments, all variations of one sentence: Do not go thinking you are anything special. He meant it as satire, a portrait [music] of small-town envy. Norway read it, laughed, winced, and then quietly adopted it as a national operating [music] manual. Janteloven, the law of Jante, was never passed by any parliament, yet it governs this society more firmly than most laws that were. It has real costs. Ambitious people can find it suffocating, and Norwegians argue about it constantly. [music] But it is also the reason a $2 trillion fortune produced no visible aristocracy. [music] In Norway, wealth is not for wearing. It is for making sure nobody has to be afraid. >> [music] >> Because that, in the end, is the answer this year has been building toward. Being rich here was never about having more. It is about fearing less. No fear of the hospital [music] bill, of the university debt, of the empty old age. The fund pays for the fearlessness of people who have not been born [music] yet. A Christmas present from 1969 that this country decided never to finish unwrapping. And so, the circle closes. January returns. The Skry come home to Lofoten, and on a snowy street at 8:00 in the morning, a 7-year-old walks to school [music] alone in the dark. Nobody worries. In the richest [music] country on Earth, that might be the only display of wealth that matters. One word. What does Norway [music] make you feel? Tell us in the comments. And if your family left [music] Norway generations ago, name the fjord or the valley they came from. We read every story. Subscribing means you never miss a year like this one.
